title: My Groom Never Showed Up on Our Wedding Day, and Then His Mother Demanded $9,000 and the Ring Back
fb_text:
MY GROOM NEVER SHOWED UP ON OUR WEDDING DAY, THEN HIS MOTHER DEMANDED HER FAMILY'S $9,000 BACK AND THE ENGAGEMENT RING

My groom never arrived on our wedding day. Then his mother sent word that she wanted her family's $9,000 returned, along with the engagement ring. Rather than call everything off, I invited all 140 guests to enjoy the dinner my father had already paid for.

Then I asked his mother whether she wanted to stay for cake.

It started when his sister appeared in the doorway of the bridal room.

She wouldn't come inside.

Her eyes stayed fixed on the floor.

"Mom says she wants the ring back today."

I was still standing there, gripping my bouquet.

"She also says our family spent nine thousand dollars."

Then she handed me a church donation envelope.

A list of expenses had been written in pencil across the back.

Rehearsal dinner: $2,100.

Honeymoon cruise: $6,900.

Total: $9,000.

There wasn't a single dollar listed for the wedding reception.

My daddy had paid for that himself.

The clock read 3:41.

The ceremony was supposed to begin at three.

Derrick had sent his brother a message of just six words.

"I can't. Tell her I'm sorry."

He hadn't even had the courage to tell me himself.

He told his brother instead.

I called him eleven times.

Every call went straight to voicemail.

Yet somehow, less than an hour later, his brother got through to him.

Derrick was sitting in his truck beside the lake.

He was perfectly fine.

He had simply decided not to come back.

Meanwhile, 140 guests were still inside the church in their finest clothes, wondering what had happened.

The organist had already played the same four hymns three times.

Daddy came into the bridal room in a brand-new suit.

It was the first suit he'd bought since Mama passed away.

"Give me two minutes and I'll get the truck," he said.

"Daddy, if somebody has to drag him back here, I don't want to marry him."

Daddy took the envelope from my hand.

He folded it carefully.

Then he slipped it into his jacket pocket.

That was when Grandma June spoke up from her folding chair.

"Raymond, what's being kept warm over at the reception hall?"

"Roast beef. Enough for a hundred and forty."

"And the band?"

"They're already there."

"Everything paid for?"

"Six thousand four hundred dollars. I settled the bill Tuesday."

Grandma looked at me and raised her cane.

"Well, there's a church full of hungry people and a perfectly good meal sitting four blocks away."

I could have sent Derrick a message telling him exactly what I thought of him.

But that wouldn't put food on anyone's plate.

Daddy turned to face me.

"That dinner is yours. I paid for my daughter, not that boy."

I stepped out of my satin wedding shoes.

Then I put on the white sneakers I'd bought for dancing later that evening.

"And nobody better cancel that band," Grandma June declared.

"I'm eighty-four years old, and nobody has ever given me a proper wedding dance."

That nearly broke me.

For the first time all afternoon, my eyes filled with tears.

Daddy walked into the sanctuary and spoke to the guests.

"The wedding will not be taking place today. But there is a dinner waiting at the VFW hall, and my daughter would still like all of you to come."

"Everybody's invited," I added. "Both families."

Old Harold rose from the fourth pew.

"Well, I've never turned down a good roast beef dinner."

By five-thirty, I was standing behind the buffet, helping serve.

I was still in my wedding dress.

White sneakers on my feet.

A big serving spoon in my hand.

Harold was the first one through the line.

He wore the same brown suit he'd worn at his own wedding.

I handed him a plate.

One of Derrick's aunts gently took my hand and pressed it to her cheek.

Then the side door beside the flags swung open.

Derrick's mother walked in.

She wore a dark dress.

Her handbag hung from one arm.

Her car keys were clenched in her other hand.

She made her way along the wall, past everyone waiting for dinner.

One conversation stopped.

Then another.

Soon the whole room was silent.

At last she reached the buffet.

She stood directly across from me, a steaming tray of roast beef between us.

"Amy Jo, I came for the ring."

Then she added, "I'd rather not have to come back."

The ring had belonged to her mother.

And it was still on my left hand.

The same hand that held the serving spoon.

All 140 people in the room seemed to be waiting to see what I would do.

Daddy began pushing his chair back from the main table.

I gave him a slight shake of my head.

Then I reached for a clean dinner plate.

What I did next left Derrick's mother speechless, and turned a wedding day that should have been the happiest of my life into one no one in that room would ever forget.

"Daddy, if somebody has to drag him back here, I don't want to marry him."

He took the envelope from my hand, folded it carefully and tucked it into his jacket pocket.

Grandma June has a plan

From her folding chair, Grandma June spoke up. "Raymond, what's being kept warm over at the reception hall?"

"Roast beef. Enough for a hundred and forty."

"And the band?"

"They're already there. I settled the bill Tuesday. Six thousand four hundred dollars."

Grandma lifted her cane. "Well, there's a church full of hungry people and a perfectly good meal sitting four blocks away."

I could have sent Derrick a message telling him exactly what I thought of him, but that wouldn't put food on anyone's plate. Daddy said, "That dinner is yours. I paid for my daughter, not that boy."

I stepped out of my satin shoes and put on the white sneakers I'd bought for dancing that night. "And nobody better cancel that band," Grandma June declared. "I'm eighty-four years old, and nobody has ever given me a proper wedding dance."

That nearly broke me. For the first time all afternoon, my eyes filled with tears.

Daddy went into the sanctuary. "The wedding will not be taking place today. But there is a dinner waiting at the VFW hall, and my daughter would still like all of you to come."

"Everybody's invited," I added. "Both families."

Old Harold stood up from the fourth pew. "Well, I've never turned down a good roast beef dinner."

The woman at the buffet

By five-thirty I was behind the buffet in my wedding dress and white sneakers, a big serving spoon in my hand. Harold came through first, in the same brown suit he'd worn at his own wedding. One of Derrick's aunts gently took my free hand and pressed it to her cheek.

Then the side door beside the flags swung open, and Derrick's mother walked in. She wore a dark dress, her handbag on one arm and her car keys clenched in her other hand. She walked along the wall, and one conversation after another went quiet until the whole room was silent.

She stopped across from me, a steaming tray of roast beef between us.

"Amy Jo, I came for the ring. I'd rather not have to come back."

It had belonged to her mother, and it was still on my left hand. All 140 people seemed to be waiting to see what I would do. Daddy began pushing back his chair. I shook my head slightly. Then I reached for a clean dinner plate.

I set the plate on the table and put down my spoon. I slid the ring off my finger and laid it gently beside the plate.

"This was your mother's, and it belongs with your family," I said. "I'm not keeping it. But you drove all this way, and nobody leaves this hall hungry. Please, sit down. Would you like to stay for cake?"

She stared at the ring, then at the plate. Her mouth opened, but nothing came out. Her keys slipped from her hand and hit the floor with a clatter. For a long moment she just stood there as the room watched.

Then her shoulders dropped. "I should never have sent that envelope," she whispered. "My son should have been standing where you are, and I was too ashamed to face it."

Daddy came over and pulled out a chair for her. She sat down. I filled her plate with roast beef, and Harold, of all people, passed her the rolls.

Later, the band struck up. Grandma June got her wedding dance, spinning slowly on the arm of my father while the whole hall clapped, and I danced in my white sneakers until my feet ached. Near the end of the night, Derrick's mother quietly asked if she could have a slice of cake, and I cut it myself.

It was not the wedding I had planned. But nobody in that room will ever forget it, and neither will I.
